newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ yields lose ground on day, still end stronger.
newsitem.headline: NZ yields lose ground on day, still end stronger.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (MAR) 92.60 (PREV 92.59) 90-DAYS 7.37 (PREV 7.42)
OVERNIGHT CASH 7.35 PCT (PREV 7.30) US 5-YR 6.10 (PREV 6.10)
* NZ yields lose ground on day but still stronger at close
* Volumes minimal
* Dec qtr retail trade data has little impact
New Zealand debt markets ended slightly stronger on Monday, but almost erased the gains made earlier on in the session.
The mid bonds ended flat at 7.22 percent, while the 11/06 maturity closed two basis points lower in yield at 7.26 percent, from its 7.23 percent open.
"A dead day. That's the best way to describe it," one bond dealer said. He saw yields moving sideways in the short term, with little to drive them higher or lower.
"The little economic news that we do have this week I don't think is going to cause too many people too much strife.

"Until we get some profile in this yield curve I think you'll find things are going to move sideways. Basically as far as the investor is concerned there's no difference between investing in the short or the long end," he said.
December quarter Labour Cost Index data is due on Friday, and building consents for December on Thursday.
Dealers said the money market got paid up a point or two on the back of retail trade data issued earlier in the session, but the impact of the data was negligible.
Real, seasonally adjusted retail sales fell 0.1 percent in the December quarter, while seasonally adjusted sales fell 1.1 percent in the December month.
One dealer said the number was mildly positive for the inflation outlook and with the recent strength of the currency's Trade-Weighted Index he would have expected a small rally.
"So it's finding a lot of resistance at this 7.30 percent on the physical bank bills, and it could gap if it gets through there, I would think."
The dealer said the normal trade-off between a higher currency and lower rates was not really occurring at this stage, but the market had been extremely thin.
"What does the currency have to do to see these bank bills rally further? The longer the TWI stays up here the tighter monetary conditions get," he said.
